0.title: Course Introduction
0.content:
Two Cabernet Francs from Chinon: one finished in stainless steel, the other sleeping two or three years in oak — once opened, two completely different worlds. This lesson is one of the most important tasting-training lessons in the Loire Valley: learning to use your nose and palate to identify the effect of the vessel on the wine is a required skill for entering the sommelier's world.

Learning Objectives

🔬 Understand how vessel type affects wine chemistry

How stainless steel, old large oak casks and new small oak barrels each change aroma, tannin and mouthfeel structure

👃 Build a tasting fingerprint for identification

Learn to identify, in blind tasting, the aroma differences of "steel-tank fresh fruit" vs "cask complexity" vs "new-barrel vanilla"

🏆 Understand the winemaking philosophy of legendary Loire estates

The differences in vessel choice and philosophy between Clos Rougeard (long ageing in new barrels) and Charles Joguet (choosing vessels by site)
1.title: The Science of Three Vessel Types
1.highlights.0.title: Stainless steel tank (Cuve Inox)
1.highlights.0.content: A sealed container with no oxidation, fully preserving primary fruit and varietal character, with crisp acidity unaffected; the first choice of modern "purist" winemaking
1.highlights.1.title: Old large oak cask (Foudre or Demi-Muid)
1.highlights.1.content: Micro-oxidation, with almost no flavour from the oak itself (old casks have already released tannin and vanilla), but slow oxidation gives the wine roundness and complexity; the first choice of Loire traditionalists
1.highlights.2.title: New small oak barrel (Barrique 225L new)
1.highlights.2.content: Intense oak vanilla, coconut, toast and clove aromas, with more tannin; new-barrel Cabernet Franc is relatively rare in the Loire, appearing almost only in experimental or top wines
1.content:
The effect of oak barrels on wine is more than simply "adding wood flavour" — it involves complex chemical and physical processes:

💨 Micro-oxygenation

The wood fibres of an oak barrel let tiny amounts of oxygen in, reacting slowly with the wine. This process softens tannins, stabilises colour and lets aromas evolve from "primary fruit" to more complex "secondary aromas" (leather, tobacco, dried flowers). Old and new barrels give similar micro-oxygenation, but the aroma input is completely different.

🔥 Toast level

When barrels are made the inner wall is toasted: Light Toast retains more oak tannin; Heavy Toast releases more vanillin and eugenol. The toast level chosen directly affects the wine's flavour.
2.title: Two Philosophies: Clos Rougeard vs Charles Joguet
2.content:
🏰 Clos Rougeard (Saumur-Champigny)

Philosophy: Burgundian long ageing in oak barrels, low intervention

Key figures: the brothers Charly and Nady Foucault (the family's winemaking history goes back to the 17th century; taken over by the Bouygues family from 2017)

Vessels: 225L oak barriques: Le Bourg uses brand-new, heavily toasted new barrels; Les Poyeux uses second-hand barrels (previously holding wine from other top estates). Not large foudres

Ageing time: Le Bourg ages about 2 years in new barrels, then about 2 more years in bottle before release

Style: extremely complex aromas (leather, dried rose, tobacco, minerals), fine but dense tannins, needing 10–20 years to show its full face. Called "the Romanée-Conti of Saumur-Champigny."

Price: top wines on the second-hand market can reach several hundred euros or more

⚗️ Charles Joguet (Chinon)

Philosophy: single sites + experiments with different vessels

Key figures: the Chinon estate founded by Charles Joguet, now managed by Alain Delaunay

Vessels: depending on the site, flexibly using stainless steel and old large oak casks, occasionally experimenting with new barrels

Core idea: let the soil speak — gravel sites in steel to keep fresh fruit, tuffeau sites in old casks to add mineral complexity

Representative wines: Clos de la Dioterie (tuffeau, old casks, complex), Varennes du Grand Clos (gravel, steel, fresh)
3.title: Tasting Training: How to Identify the Vessel
3.content:
When tasting Chinon or Bourgueil, the following indicators help you identify the vessel used:

👃 Aroma identification

VesselAroma indicatorsIntensity
Stainless steelFresh strawberry, raspberry, violet, green pepper (if present)Pure, direct, fruit-led
Old large oak caskDried flowers, tobacco leaf, leather, minerals, smokeComplex, layered, needs time to unfold
New small oak barrelVanilla, coconut, toast, cloveObvious, may mask varietal aroma

👅 Palate identification

  • Stainless steel: crisp tannins, crisp acidity, clean finish; best "opened and drunk right away"
  • Old large oak cask: rounder tannins, silkier texture, longer finish; "needs waiting" to show
  • New small oak barrel: more tannin (oak tannin stacked on top), heavier mouthfeel, obvious woodiness

💡 Blind-tasting tip: if you smell obvious "vanilla + coconut," it is usually new oak; if it is "fresh berries + florals-led" with a crisp palate, usually stainless steel; if it is "complex leather + minerals + dried flowers" with a rounded texture, usually old casks.
4.title: Quiz
4.questions.0.question: What is the main stylistic characteristic of Cabernet Franc made in stainless steel (Cuve Inox)?
4.questions.0.options.0: Intense vanilla and coconut, rich tannins
4.questions.0.options.1: Preserves the purest primary fruit (strawberry, violet), crisp acidity, suited to drinking young
4.questions.0.options.2: Complex leather and tobacco, needing 10 years of ageing
4.questions.0.options.3: Oxidative style with nutty and beeswax aromas
4.questions.0.explanation: Stainless steel completely excludes oxygen, preserving the purest primary fruit of the wine (varietal character and fermentation aromas) with crisp acidity unaffected; it is the first choice of "purist" winemaking and very suited to early-drinking wines that emphasise varietal personality.
4.questions.1.question: Why is Clos Rougeard called "the Romanée-Conti of Saumur-Champigny"?
4.questions.1.options.0: It uses exactly the same Pinot Noir variety
4.questions.1.options.1: New-barrel long ageing, extremely low yields, top wines priced very high on the second-hand market, with complexity and ageing potential at the level of top Burgundy
4.questions.1.options.2: It is located in a Grand Cru site of Saumur-Champigny
4.questions.1.options.3: It is the only Loire AOC allowed to use Pinot Noir
4.questions.1.explanation: Clos Rougeard (the Foucault brothers) ages for a long time in 225L oak barrels (Le Bourg in brand-new, heavily toasted new barrels) with extremely low yields; its complexity and ageing potential reach world-class level (the top wine Le Bourg needs 10–20 years of ageing) and it is priced very high on the second-hand market, one of the Loire's most legendary reds.
